sources.site: Artemis Base Camp, Shackleton Crater Rim

decisions.title: EVA Crew Recall & Ice Core Protocol
decisions.situation: Specialist Leo and Dr. Maya are 900m away at the drill site with 4 fresh pressurized ice cores.

options.label: Emergency Sprint (Abandon Equipment)
options.feedback: Crew reached the airlock quickly. The drill rig and all 4 ice cores were left behind.

options.label: Pack Rover & Secure Cores
options.feedback: All 4 ice cores secured in rover cold storage, but the crew absorbed +22 mSv during the operation.

decisions.title: Habitat Storm Shielding Setup
decisions.situation: Regolith cover alone is insufficient for an X-class proton storm. Choose an active shielding protocol.

options.label: Pump Hydroponic Water-Wall
options.feedback: Hydrogen in the water bladders absorbed 65% of incoming protons. Greenhouse crops wilted.

options.label: Overcharge Magnetic Deflector
options.feedback: Magnetic shield deflected 85% of charged particles, but main battery bank is critically depleted.

options.label: Regolith Shelter Only
options.feedback: No resources consumed, but high-energy protons penetrated the habitat ceiling.

decisions.title: Critical Grid & Solar Array Protocol
decisions.situation: Initial proton showers are striking the rim. Unprotected solar arrays risk electrostatic burnout.

options.label: Retract Panels & Isolate Grid
options.feedback: Panels safely housed in vaults. Outpost runs strictly on remaining battery reserves.

options.label: Keep Arrays Deployed for Heaters
options.feedback: Auxiliary life support stayed active, but static charges caused minor electrical fires.

ending_a.title: The Exemplary Commander
ending_a.description: Dr. Maya and Specialist Leo survived the X-class storm with minimal radiation. All 4 ice cores were preserved in cold storage.
ending_a.nasaFact: Water and polyethylene shielding are primary candidates for Artemis habitats because hydrogen atoms efficiently absorb solar protons.

ending_b.title: Survival Over Science
ending_b.description: The crew reached safety and the habitat stayed intact, but abandoning the ice samples delayed lunar water research milestones.
ending_b.nasaFact: Lunar polar ice is essential for future missions because it can be split into hydrogen for rocket fuel and oxygen for breathing.

ending_c.title: The Pyrrhic Discovery
ending_c.description: Scientific samples were secured, but the crew took an elevated radiation dose that triggered acute fatigue and medical quarantine.
ending_c.nasaFact: NASA OSDR data (Study OSD-379) shows space radiation damages DNA and immune function, making exposure tracking a top mission priority.

ending_d.title: Outpost Power Failure
ending_d.description: Battery reserves hit 0% during the storm. Thermal heaters failed, forcing an emergency abort to the Orion capsule.
ending_d.nasaFact: Nighttime temperatures at the lunar poles reach -130°C. Power management is a non-negotiable life support requirement.

educationalTooltips.mSv: MilliSievert (mSv) measures radiation dose. On Earth, we get about 3 mSv per year. Astronauts must stay below 50 mSv per mission.
educationalTooltips.CME: A Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) is a billion tons of super-hot solar plasma hurled into space by magnetic explosions on the Sun.
educationalTooltips.WaterWall: Water molecules (H2O) are packed with light hydrogen protons, making them one of the best shields against space radiation.
